segments.text: When you type a message to an AI like ChatGPT, the system doesn't actually read English.
Instead, it breaks your text into small, discrete pieces called tokens.
Every token starts with an embedding, a specific row of numbers, that represents its baseline
dictionary meaning, before the AI considers the rest of the sentence.
In this first panel, we see the challenge of ambiguous language.
The word light can mean brightness, as in turn on the light, or it can describe weight, as
in a suitcase that is light enough to carry.
The second panel shows a similar issue with pronouns.
A single word like it changes its meaning entirely based on the words around it.
It refers to the cat if the cat is thirsty, but it refers to the milk if the milk is fresh.
The only way to determine which meaning fits is to look at the surrounding words, the
context.
While this is intuitive for humans, historically it has been one of the most difficult tasks
for AI to master.
This flowchart shows how earlier AI systems processed text.
They read sequentially, moving one word at a time from left to right.
In this example, the AI has to carry the information from the word cat all the way
through a long string of interrupting words before it finally reaches the word it.
This sequential assembly line method was inefficient.
In longer passages, older models would frequently lose the connection between related words,
because the distance between them was simply too great to track.
In 2017, researchers at Google published a paper called Attention is All You Need.
It introduced the transformer, the architecture that provides the T in chat GPT.
Unlike previous models, the transformer reads your whole message at once.
As seen in this cluster, all words are available simultaneously.
Because they arrive together, GPT instantly draws context from cat, bypassing the words
in between.
Having every word present from the start solves the problem of distance.
However, the AI still needs a mathematical way to determine which of these words actually
matter to each other.
To build a specific meaning, the model must update the starting numbers of a token by
looking at its neighbors.
This happens through two mathematical steps.
The first step is attention.
The model weighs information from relevant words, blending it into the numbers for it.
Next is transformation.
The model takes those blended numbers and uses learned patterns to refine them into
a context-aware representation.
Attention and transformation work together in a loop.
By constantly updating the token's numbers, the AI dynamically rewrites a word's raw
meaning into a rich situational one.
Let's apply this mechanism.
Pause and look at these sentences.
Can you spot the words that signal the correct meaning?
In the first panel, turn on and carry provide context, signaling the AI to update light for
brightness or weight.
In the second panel, the words thirsty and fresh act as the critical weights.
They determine whether the attention of the word it should point toward the cat or toward
the milk.
This process of weighting relationships allows the AI to move far beyond literal dictionary
definitions.
By mapping how words interact across an entire message, the model can resolve these simple
ambiguities and eventually handle the more complex logic found in sarcasm and idioms.
Reading everything at once solves the context problem, but it creates a new flaw.
The model loses the order of the words.
Consider these three tokens.
Dog bites man, and man bites dog use the exact same words and starting embeddings,
but the order completely changes what happened.
To fix this, the transformer uses positional encoding, applying numerical position stamps
to tell the system exactly where every token belongs.
Positional encoding acts as the structural glue.
It ensures that even though the AI absorbs the sentence all at once, it still preserves
the critical meaning that comes from human word order.
Attention is all you need.
AI uses relationships between words to help interpret your message.
